## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

*Architecture stack focus for this chapter.*

_What does mastering the full stack enable that expertise in any single layer cannot?_

A single production decision travels through the entire stack. A data pipeline decides which events count as training signal. That signal shapes the architecture, which in turn fixes memory footprint and arithmetic intensity. Those properties constrain hardware choice, quantization strategy, serving latency, drift monitoring, and governance obligations. Mastered individually, each layer represents a valuable skill; mastered together, they confer the ability to reason across boundaries that no single specialty sees in full. An engineer who understands only compression can shrink a model, but cannot predict whether the accuracy loss matters for the deployment context. An engineer who understands only serving can optimize latency, but cannot trace a performance regression to a data pipeline change three stages upstream. Many of the costliest production failures arise at these boundaries, where every component passes its local tests yet the system as a whole misses its target. In D·A·M terms, what endures is the ability to analyze a system before it is built, reasoning about how data, algorithm, and machine constraints will interact, where bottlenecks will emerge, and which architectural commitments will prove irreversible. The constraints that govern these interactions outlive any specific framework, hardware generation, or model family, because the cost of moving data, the speed of light, and the gap between an assumed and a measured bottleneck do not turn over with them. Thinking in systems rather than components separates an engineer who can build a part from one who can build the whole.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Trace how data, architecture, compression, hardware, serving, operations, and governance decisions propagate constraints across an ML system
- Apply lighthouse-model reasoning to diagnose bottlenecks across cloud, mobile, edge, recommendation, and TinyML deployments
- Synthesize core ML systems principles into a framework for reasoning across Data, Algorithm, and Machine constraints
- Evaluate deployment trade-offs using latency budgets, memory and energy movement, drift, and responsibility constraints
- Justify an engineering approach for emerging contexts such as embodied, composed, and multi-node systems, using cross-layer evidence to identify where single-node reasoning must widen its boundary

:::

## The System Is the Model {#sec-synthesizing-ml-systems-ee10}

**The system is the model**\index{System is the model, The!definition}, meaning that the behavior a user receives from a machine learning service is produced by the data pipeline, the trained weights, the execution stack, the serving path, and the monitoring loop together, never by the weights alone. The request that opened the introduction shows the claim in miniature. When a user asks a smartphone voice assistant a question, learned components convert speech to text, interpret intent, retrieve information, and generate a response within seconds (@sec-introduction-ai-moment-37f1), and every chapter since has given one stage of that request a mechanism and a cost. @Sec-responsible-engineering added the last constraint the book imposes, the obligations a system owes the people it affects, and showed that it behaves like the latency and memory budgets before it, because it can be met only where every upstream stage preserved the freedom to meet it. Each constraint was taught one layer at a time. The costliest failures arise where the layers meet.

A composite scenario, extending the calibration pitfall analyzed in @sec-model-serving-fallacies-pitfalls-336b rather than reporting any one incident, shows such a failure. A team deploys an image classification model to a fleet of mobile devices. The architecture team chose depthwise separable convolutions to factorize spatial filtering from channel projection, reducing arithmetic operations. The compression team quantized weights and activations to INT8 to cut memory traffic and fit within on-chip static RAM (SRAM). The serving team met a p99 latency target of 50 ms. Each team succeeded by its local metric, yet within weeks, accuracy dropped by four percentage points on specific firmware and device cohorts. INT8 quantization fixes its clipping ranges during quantization-range calibration, permanently encoding the statistical distribution of the calibration images. A firmware-specific preprocessing routine interpolated images differently and presented an altered input distribution to the quantized model on those cohorts. No component failed in isolation, and nothing crashed. Each team validated its component against standard inputs, and while latency was evaluated end to end along the deployed request path, accuracy was measured only as an aggregate scalar over an offline evaluation set, so users on the affected cohorts simply received worse predictions that the system's monitoring was never built to see. Heterogeneous edge environments require disaggregated cohort monitoring from day one.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol1_conclusion_margin_001.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical causal chain: INT8 calibration, then the firmware preprocessing path, then an input shift on one device cohort, ending in an accuracy drop marked in red."}

*A calibration choice surfaces as a cohort accuracy drop three stages downstream.*
:::

Most failures of this kind start at an interface between components, so the main task is to test the interfaces before they fail. Traditional software engineering treats functional correctness as decoupled from the underlying hardware; in machine learning systems, statistical behavior is physically inseparable from the pipelines, memory hierarchies, and accelerators that train, serve, and monitor the model. The bitter lesson teaches that general methods scaling with computation outrun hand-encoded heuristics (@sec-introduction-bitter-lesson-79c7).

Affording that scale is the job of the iron law of ML systems\index{Iron law of ML systems!synthesis} (principle \ref{pri-iron-law}), which sits at the center of this discipline. Its three terms (data movement, compute, and overhead) serve as the primary engineering levers for quantitative analysis. Building intelligence requires both statistical algorithms and adherence to the silicon contract\index{Silicon contract!constraint propagation} (principle \ref{pri-silicon-contract}), the requirement that the resource a model saturates first be the one the executing machine supplies in abundance. Arithmetic intensity and roofline modeling convert qualitative performance intuitions into quantitative upper bounds [@williams2009].

System capabilities emerge from co-design across the Data, Algorithm, and Machine (D·A·M) triad rather than from isolated algorithmic breakthroughs, and success and failure arise from the same mechanism, cross-layer coupling. The transformer architecture [@vaswani2017] scaled into models such as GPT-3 and Llama 2 [@brown2020language; @touvron2023llama2] only because decisions in other layers made attention affordable: IO-aware attention kernels that keep intermediate scores in on-chip memory, low-precision tensor units that raise the peak arithmetic rate, and partitioning of tensor state across accelerators.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ IO-aware attention tiling, which keeps attention scores in on-chip memory, is established in @sec-model-training-flash-attention-ioaware-attention-optimization-3da0.
:::

Integration has concrete consequences. Software engineering often treats the "model" as a weights checkpoint, a single file of floating-point numbers. In a production environment, however, the weights are only one component of the true model, and often not the most fragile. A model that produces high benchmark accuracy fails if it ingests corrupted features, and a model that converges cleanly during training fails if it cannot satisfy deployment latency constraints.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The finding that model code is a small fraction of a production ML system, whose surrounding pipelines, serving, and monitoring are larger and more enduring, is established in @sec-introduction-datacentric-paradigm-shift-4eca.
:::

::: {#chk-conclusion-systems-thinking .callout-checkpoint title="Systems thinking"}

The system's dependencies, feedback loops, and request path make its boundaries testable.

**The integration**

- [ ] **Dependencies**: can you trace a data-pipeline change through training and serving to identify its latency effect?
- [ ] **Feedback loops**: have you mapped how the model's predictions influence its future training data?

**The holism**

- [ ] **End-to-end**: can you trace a user request from the user interface, through the network, preprocessing, model, postprocessing, and back to the user interface?

:::

Tracing a request end to end shows the structure behind this. Every layer of the stack enforces physical and statistical constraints on the next. Data curation and selection bound what the learner sees; architectures, training systems, and frameworks lower the resulting computation onto hardware; compression, acceleration, and benchmarking move the physical boundaries; and serving, operations, and responsible engineering hold the result to tail-latency budgets, drift, and subgroup outcomes in production. Because these stages form a tightly coupled system rather than a sequence of isolated handoffs, engineering decisions never remain localized, and an engineer who optimizes a single layer in isolation cannot predict how the change will propagate.

The rest of the chapter makes that claim quantitative. The five lighthouse models come first, each traced from its home regime to the lever that paid off and the lever that was wasted. The thirteen quantitative principles follow, regrouped by the three questions the introduction asked of every ML system: what shapes its predictions, what limits its execution, and what evidence supports its deployment. The dual mandate is then measured on two lighthouses, DLRM for trustworthy behavior and the GPT-2 family for physical deliverability. The same principles then forecast where constraints bind next, from microcontrollers to composed services and fleets. The chapter closes on the responsibility that follows from building such systems, the cross-boundary forms of the book's recurring mistakes, and a final trace of the voice-assistant request through every layer.

## Lighthouse Models: Constraint Propagation {#sec-conclusion-lighthouse-constraint-propagation}

```{=latex}
\newpage
```

The five lighthouse models\index{Lighthouse model!bottleneck probe} each have a home regime, the binding resource it exposes under its typical operating conditions. ResNet-50 is compute-bound, GPT-2 and Llama decode is bandwidth-bound, DLRM is capacity-bound, MobileNetV2 is compute-bound in its efficient regime, and keyword spotting (KWS) is power-bound. Across the book, each lighthouse rewarded the lever aimed at its binding term and wasted the effort aimed anywhere else (@tbl-lighthouse-trace).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The five lighthouse models and their diagnostic execution regimes are established in @sec-introduction-lighthouse-models-9b1c.
:::

| **Lighthouse**             | **Home Regime**                       | **Binding Term**                                                                   | **Lever That Paid**                                                                         | **Lever Wasted**                                                                              |
|:---------------------------|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **ResNet-50**              | Compute-bound                         | Compute, $\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)$                             | Batching that reuses filter weights across inputs; reduced-precision tensor arithmetic      | More memory bandwidth once batched convolutions sit right of the ridge point                  |
| **GPT-2/Llama decode**     | Bandwidth-bound                       | Data movement, $\DataVolume/\Bandwidth$                                            | Batching across requests; fewer bytes per weight; managing the per-request key-value cache  | More peak arithmetic throughput, or compute-only kernel tuning at batch one                   |
| **DLRM**                   | Capacity-bound                        | Memory capacity, a precondition before any term applies                            | Placing and sharding embedding tables across memory tiers; caching frequently accessed rows | Faster dense arithmetic for the small fully connected layers                                  |
| **MobileNetV2**            | Compute-bound in its efficient regime | Compute within a phone's power envelope; depthwise layers cross to bandwidth-bound | Depthwise separable convolutions, then INT8 once depthwise layers became bandwidth-bound    | Further operation cuts on layers already bound by bandwidth                                   |
| **Keyword spotting (KWS)** | Power-bound                           | Energy per inference within a milliwatt budget                                     | A sub-megabyte INT8 model with a tensor arena planned at build time                         | Streaming audio to the cloud, whose radio transmission costs more energy than local inference |

: **Lighthouse Constraint Traces**: Each lighthouse probes one home regime, and the lever that paid off was the one aimed at that regime's binding term. A regime describes a workload on a machine rather than a model name, so a lighthouse crosses regimes when batch size, phase, or precision changes. {#tbl-lighthouse-trace tbl-colwidths="[13,15,22,27,23]"}

The regime belongs to the workload on a machine, so the same model can change regime, and the regime has to be checked before an optimization is chosen. GPT-2\index{GPT-2!memory bandwidth} training is compute-bound even though its decode is bandwidth-bound, because a training step reuses each weight across every token in the batch. ResNet-50\index{ResNet-50!batching efficiency} became input-bound in @sec-model-training when the data pipeline could not keep the accelerator fed, and INT8 arithmetic, which doubles the H100's peak rate without raising its memory bandwidth, doubles the ridge point, which leaves some ResNet-50 layers below it and bandwidth-bound. DLRM\index{DLRM!capacity-bound workload} shows the same pattern at the large end of the deployment spectrum, where embedding capacity decides which term binds; MobileNetV2\index{MobileNetV2!efficiency under constraint} and keyword spotting\index{Keyword spotting!sub-megabyte models} show it at the small end, where thermal and power envelopes do. A larger recommendation model, a larger decoder, or a faster vision network differs from its lighthouse in scale, not in which term binds, so the diagnosis carries forward to models that do not yet exist.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MOBILENET JOURNEY MATH
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-lighthouse-journey-mobilenet (Architecture and Compression rows)
# │          in the Lighthouse Models section.
# │
# │ Goal:    Compute the FLOP and byte ratios that quantify MobileNetV2's
# │          efficiency wins across the architecture/compression journey.
# │ Show:    Depthwise-separable FLOP reduction, ResNet-50 vs. MobileNetV2
# │          operation ratio, and INT8 byte ratios versus FP32/FP16.
# │ How:     Apply the depthwise-separable FLOP formula at a representative
# │          3x3, 256-channel layer; divide ResNet-50/MobileNetV2 inference
# │          FLOPs; divide FP32/FP16 byte widths by INT8 byte width.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check

class MobileNetJourneyMath:
    # LOAD
    resnet = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    mobilenet = Models.Vision.MobileNetV2
    kernel_size = 3
    representative_output_channels = 256

    # EXECUTE
    standard_to_depthwise = (kernel_size**2 * representative_output_channels) / (kernel_size**2 + representative_output_channels)
    resnet_to_mobilenet = resnet.inference_flops / mobilenet.inference_flops
    int8_vs_fp32 = BYTES_FP32 / BYTES_INT8
    int8_vs_fp16 = BYTES_FP16 / BYTES_INT8

    # GUARD
    check(8 <= standard_to_depthwise <= 9, "Depthwise separable example should land near 8--9x.")
    check(13 <= resnet_to_mobilenet.to("").magnitude <= 15, "ResNet-50/MobileNetV2 ratio drifted.")
    check(int8_vs_fp32.to("").magnitude == 4 and int8_vs_fp16.to("").magnitude == 2, "INT8 byte ratios changed.")

    # OUTPUT
    depthwise_reduction_mult_str = fmt_multiple(standard_to_depthwise, precision=1, commas=False)
    resnet_ops_reduction_mult_str = fmt_multiple(resnet_to_mobilenet.to("").magnitude, precision=1, commas=False)
    int8_fp32_reduction_mult_str = fmt_multiple(int8_vs_fp32.to("").magnitude, precision=0, commas=False)
    int8_fp16_reduction_mult_str = fmt_multiple(int8_vs_fp16.to("").magnitude, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Applying each phase of the book to MobileNetV2 shows how cross-layer constraints converge on a single engineering artifact (@tbl-lighthouse-journey-mobilenet). Across nine phases, from the deployment tier's envelope through architecture, training, data selection, compression, acceleration, benchmarking, serving, and runtime operations, each engineering decision narrows the options available downstream.

| **Journey Phase**                             | **System Lens**                | **MobileNetV2 Implementation**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|:----------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Foundations (@sec-ml-systems)**             | Deployment Tier Constraints    | Mobile tier sets a watt-scale power, thermal, and battery envelope that every later phase must respect                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Architecture (@sec-network-architectures)** | Algorithmic Efficiency         | Depthwise Separable Convolutions: `{python} MobileNetJourneyMath.depthwise_reduction_mult_str` fewer FLOPs for a representative 3-by-3, 256-output-channel layer and `{python} MobileNetJourneyMath.resnet_ops_reduction_mult_str` fewer operations than ResNet-50 at ImageNet scale |
| **Training (@sec-model-training)**            | Throughput vs. Latency         | Trained at high-throughput batch sizes for a model that will serve single requests at low latency                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Data Selection (@sec-data-selection)**      | Capacity-Matched Augmentation  | Milder augmentation matched to a compact network's limited capacity, validated against deployment invariances such as device and lighting variation, at no inference cost                                                                                                            |
| **Compression (@sec-model-compression)**      | Navigating the Pareto Frontier | INT8 Quantization: FP32 uses `{python} MobileNetJourneyMath.int8_fp32_reduction_mult_str` and FP16 uses `{python} MobileNetJourneyMath.int8_fp16_reduction_mult_str` the per-value storage of INT8, with accuracy revalidated per deployment                                         |
| **Acceleration (@sec-hardware-acceleration)** | Honoring the Silicon Contract  | Mapping kernels to mobile neural processing units (NPUs) (for example, Apple Neural Engine) to maximize hardware execution efficiency                                                                                                                                                |
| **Benchmarking (@sec-benchmarking)**          | Component vs. End-to-End       | Confirming that compression and accelerator gains survive the full pipeline by separating accelerator latency from preprocessing and transfer, and rechecking INT8 accuracy on edge cases such as unusual lighting                                                                   |
| **Serving (@sec-model-serving)**              | Respecting the Latency Budget  | $\text{p99} < 50$ ms constraint; optimizing preprocessing (resize/normalize) to avoid CPU bottlenecks                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Operations (@sec-ml-operations)**           | Managing System Entropy        | Drift Monitoring: Detecting distribution shifts and tracking cohort-level accuracy across heterogeneous device populations and lighting conditions                                                                                                                                   |

: **The Lighthouse Journey (MobileNetV2)**: Applying the book's nine phases to one model shows how decisions in one domain (for example, architecture) propagate constraints and opportunities into downstream domains (for example, hardware acceleration and monitoring). {#tbl-lighthouse-journey-mobilenet tbl-colwidths="[17,22,61]"}

Decisions in one row constrain options in the next. Depthwise separable convolutions cut the operation count, but depthwise filtering reduces cross-channel reuse and often leaves these layers bandwidth-bound on mobile hardware. When profiling confirms that regime, a further cut in operations buys little, and the compression row's reduction in bytes per value becomes the next lever. That lever pays only if the acceleration row confirms that the mobile NPU executes those INT8 operators, and only if the benchmarking row shows the gain surviving preprocessing and transfer. The same propagation runs through every lighthouse, and reasoning about it before profiling requires the quantitative principles the book accumulated part by part.

## Thirteen Quantitative Principles {#sec-thirteen-quantitative-invariants-0dd2}

When an engineer alters an embedding table layout, doubles batch size, or quantizes an attention layer from FP16 to INT8, the performance outcome is not random; it is governed by physical bounds, empirical trade-offs, and operational feedback. Reasoning quantitatively about this behavior across the entire stack requires analytical tools with stated assumptions, and the book accumulated **thirteen quantitative principles**\index{Thirteen quantitative principles!framework} for that purpose across its four parts (@tbl-thirteen-principles). They are not all the same kind of statement. Three are hard bounds (the Pareto frontier, the arithmetic intensity law, and Amdahl's Law), two are decompositions (the iron law and the energy-movement principle), two are fitted models (statistical drift and bias feedback), two are policies whose parameters a product decision sets (the verification gap and the latency budget), and four are heuristics (data-as-code, data gravity, the silicon contract, and training-serving skew). The heuristic label marks the silicon contract as a prediction about which resource an architecture saturates first, a prediction that the arithmetic intensity bound then tests. Each principle box on the part pages names its kind, and each principle is reliable only within its stated assumptions.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-energy-movement-math
#| output: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ENERGY-MOVEMENT PRINCIPLE RATIOS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-thirteen-principles (energy-movement principle row) and the
# │          adjacent diagnostic-chain paragraph in the Thirteen Quantitative
# │          Invariants section.
# │
# │ Goal:    Quantify the energy cost of a DRAM access relative to a single
# │          FP32 or FP16 floating-point operation.
# │ Show:    DRAM-vs-FP32 and DRAM-vs-FP16 energy ratios used to anchor the
# │          "100--1,000x" energy-movement claim in prose.
# │ How:     Divide the reference DRAM access energy by the per-FLOP energy
# │          constants for FP32 and FP16 from mlsysim.core.units.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import flop
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt, fmt_multiple, fmt_multiple_range, check

class EnergyMovementMath:
    # LOAD
    ENERGY_DRAM_ACCESS_PJ = Hardware.Tech.Memory.DRAM.energy_per_access
    ENERGY_FLOP_FP32_PJ = Hardware.Tech.Op.FlopFp32.energy
    ENERGY_FLOP_FP16_PJ = Hardware.Tech.Op.FlopFp16.energy
    dram_access = ENERGY_DRAM_ACCESS_PJ
    fp32_flop_energy = ENERGY_FLOP_FP32_PJ * flop
    fp16_flop_energy = ENERGY_FLOP_FP16_PJ * flop

    # EXECUTE
    dram_vs_fp32 = (dram_access / fp32_flop_energy).to("").magnitude
    dram_vs_fp16 = (dram_access / fp16_flop_energy).to("").magnitude

    # GUARD
    check(100 <= dram_vs_fp32 <= 1000, "DRAM/FP32 energy ratio left expected range.")
    check(100 <= dram_vs_fp16 <= 1000, "DRAM/FP16 energy ratio left expected range.")

    # OUTPUT
    dram_vs_fp32_display = round(dram_vs_fp32)
    dram_vs_fp16_display = round(dram_vs_fp16)
    dram_vs_fp32_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dram_vs_fp32_display, precision=0, commas=False)
    dram_vs_fp16_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dram_vs_fp16_display, precision=0, commas=False)
    dram_vs_range_mult_str = fmt_multiple_range(
        dram_vs_fp32_display,
        dram_vs_fp16_display,
        precision=0,
        commas=False,
    )
```

| **#**                           | **Principle**                    | **Part**          | **Core Equation/Statement**                                                                                                                                                                    | **What It Predicts**                                                                       |
|:--------------------------------|:---------------------------------|:------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| \ref{pri-data-as-code}          | Data-as-Code Principle           | I: Foundations    | Learned behavior $\approx\text{Train}$(training data, training procedure)                                                                                                                      | Data changes behavior; other inputs also matter                                            |
| \ref{pri-data-gravity}          | Data-Gravity Principle           | I: Foundations    | Move compute toward data when repeated transfer costs exceed placement costs                                                                                                                   | Depends on volume, reuse, network, and compute mobility                                    |
| \ref{pri-iron-law}              | Iron Law of ML Systems           | II: Development   | $\Time=\DataVolume/\Bandwidth+\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)+\Latency$; overlap ranges from max to sum                                                                            | Stages may add or overlap                                                                  |
| \ref{pri-silicon-contract}      | Silicon Contract                 | II: Development   | Each architecture saturates one resource (compute, bandwidth, or capacity) first                                                                                                               | Design must target the resource saturated first                                            |
| \ref{pri-pareto-frontier}       | Pareto Frontier                  | III: Optimization | No feasible point is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on one                                                                                                            | Along the frontier, improving one objective worsens another                                |
| \ref{pri-arithmetic-intensity}  | Arithmetic Intensity Law         | III: Optimization | $\AttainableComputeRate \le \min(\PeakRate,\; \ArithmeticIntensity \times \Bandwidth)$                                                                                                         | More compute cannot raise a bandwidth ceiling                                              |
| \ref{pri-energy-movement}       | Energy-Movement Principle        | III: Optimization | $\TotalEnergy\approx \DataVolume\times \EnergyPerByteMoved+\Operations\times \EnergyPerOperation$; dynamic RAM (DRAM) to FLOP cost ratio: `{python} EnergyMovementMath.dram_vs_range_mult_str` | Total energy depends on bytes moved, operations, and per-event costs                       |
| \ref{pri-amdahl}                | Amdahl's Law                     | III: Optimization | $\text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1-\ParallelFraction) + \frac{\ParallelFraction}{\AcceleratedFractionSpeedup}}$                                                                                     | For fixed work, the serial fraction caps parallelism gains                                 |
| \ref{pri-verification-gap}      | Verification Gap                 | IV: Deployment    | Deployment-population success probability must meet the specified target at the stated task-error tolerance                                                                                    | Specify distance, tolerance, population, and required success probability                  |
| \ref{pri-statistical-drift}     | Statistical Drift Diagnostic     | IV: Deployment    | $\AccuracyAfterDeployment(\DeploymentAge)\approx\InitialAccuracy-\FittedSensitivity\cdot\StatisticalDivergence$                                                                                | A local fit; drift need not lower quality                                                  |
| \ref{pri-training-serving-skew} | Training-Serving Skew Diagnostic | IV: Deployment    | $\TrainingServingSkew=\mathbb{E}[\lvert \ServingPathPredictor(\ModelInput)-\TrainingPathPredictor(\ModelInput)\rvert]$                                                                         | Output mismatch signals risk, not accuracy loss                                            |
| \ref{pri-latency-budget}        | Latency Budget Principle         | IV: Deployment    | $\Pr[\EndToEndRequestLatency\le \CompletionDeadline]\ge \TargetCompletionQuantile$, where $\EndToEndRequestLatency$ sums the request-path delays                                               | The product SLO selects $\TargetCompletionQuantile$ and the deadline $\CompletionDeadline$ |
| \ref{pri-bias-feedback}         | Bias Feedback Model              | IV: Deployment    | $\GroupDisparity(\FeedbackIntervalCount)\approx\GroupDisparity(0)\BiasFeedbackFactor^\FeedbackIntervalCount$ with fitted $\BiasFeedbackFactor$                                                 | Feedback may amplify harm; measure and intervene                                           |

: **Thirteen Quantitative Principles**: Each tool appears in the part where its governing constraint or diagnostic use first becomes visible. The collection combines bounds, decompositions, fitted models, policy requirements, and heuristics. Each row holds under its stated assumptions; together they provide a shared analytical vocabulary for system design, optimization, and deployment. {#tbl-thirteen-principles tbl-colwidths="[3,15,13,39,30]"}

*Notation Guide for @tbl-thirteen-principles*: In deployment models, $\TaskDistance$ is the task-specific distance metric, $\TaskErrorTolerance$ is the acceptable error tolerance threshold, $\TargetCompletionQuantile$ is the target success probability for latency deadline $\CompletionDeadline$, and $\BiasFeedbackFactor$ is the amplification factor compounding disparity $\GroupDisparity$ at step $\FeedbackIntervalCount$. The drift row restates the degradation equation (@eq-degradation), in which $\FittedSensitivity$ is the sensitivity fitted from labeled outcomes and $\StatisticalDivergence$ measures how far the current input distribution has moved from the training distribution. $\TrainingServingSkew$ is the expected absolute difference between serving-path and training-path outputs on the same input. In efficiency bounds, $\AcceleratedFractionSpeedup$ is the speedup factor applied to the parallelizable fraction $\ParallelFraction$. Finite tests estimate the deployment success probability with uncertainty; an evaluation must separately state the statistical confidence level of its interval or bound.

The thirteen principles are not independent axioms. The conservation-of-complexity heuristic\index{Conservation of complexity!meta-principle}[^fn-conservation-complexity-heuristic] introduced in Part I connects them into an integrated framework. In Part III, model compression demonstrated this trade-off at the scale of a single model: pruning sacrifices capacity, quantization sacrifices precision, and distillation expends training compute. At the scale of the entire system, the engineering discipline remains identical: following any local simplification, trace where the displaced complexity has migrated. The heuristic serves as a diagnostic rather than a physical conservation law. While thoughtful design can eliminate accidental complexity outright, systemic complexity often shifts elsewhere, as when quantizing a model moves it into validation.

[^fn-conservation-complexity-heuristic]: **Conservation-of-complexity heuristic**\index{Conservation of complexity!heuristic limits}: Tesler's Law\index{Tesler's law!conservation of complexity}, a design aphorism, says that an application's irreducible complexity must be handled somewhere in the interaction among user, application, and platform [@tesler1984complexity]; extending it to all ML-system complexity is an analogy, not a physical law. Quantization may add validation burden, and abstraction may move implementation detail behind an interface, but good design can also remove accidental complexity outright. Large language model application pipelines illustrate a possible shift: simplifying the user-facing interface with shorter or vaguer prompts may move work into system prompts, retrieval, or output verification. Use the heuristic to search for displaced costs, not to assume that an equal compensating cost must exist.

The part pages introduced the principles in the order the book needed them. Read together, they sort more usefully by the three questions the introduction asked of every ML system (@sec-introduction-summary-385d): what shapes its predictions, what limits its execution, and what evidence supports its deployment. The three groupings that follow keep each principle's number, so every principle can still be found on its part page.

### What shapes predictions (principles 1 and 13) {.unnumbered}

The data-as-code principle\index{Data-as-code principle!logical program} (\ref{pri-data-as-code}) answers the first question directly. The training dataset dictates learned behavior, so a modification to data curation is a behavioral change requiring the same rigorous versioning, code review, and regression testing applied to source code. The bias feedback model\index{Bias feedback model!disparity amplification} (principle \ref{pri-bias-feedback}) extends that answer past launch, because a deployed model's predictions shape the data its successor trains on. It treats disparity as a quantity that compounds across retraining cycles at a fitted rate, which turns fairness into a stability question about the deployment loop. An automated credit model may satisfy throughput and convergence targets while systematically compounding disparities against underserved groups, so the feedback loop must be intercepted by disaggregated monitoring rather than discovered in aggregate accuracy.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The bias feedback model, with the fitted factor that projects when a disparity that passed its release gate will breach it, is established in @sec-responsible-engineering-monitoring-incident-response-54f4.
:::

### What limits execution (principles 2–8) {.unnumbered}

The data-gravity principle\index{Data gravity principle!physical anchor} (\ref{pri-data-gravity}) opens the second question, because data volume dictates where computation must execute. Moving a petabyte-scale dataset between cloud regions costs days of transfer time and substantial egress fees, which readily justifies moving compute to the data rather than the reverse.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The transfer time and egress cost that make a large dataset the gravitational center of an architecture are established in @sec-data-engineering-data-gravity-adcb.
:::

The lighthouse models carry the same placement constraint into execution. In DLRM, embedding tables that outgrow a single accelerator's memory make memory capacity a binding design constraint, requiring the execution system to be engineered around where the parameters physically reside. Compute-to-data placement recurs across deployment environments precisely because moving large, low-reuse datasets saturates interconnects.

The iron law (principle \ref{pri-iron-law}) and the silicon contract (principle \ref{pri-silicon-contract}) govern execution efficiency. The iron law's three-term decomposition isolates data movement, computation, and overhead; the silicon contract reveals which term limits performance on a given architecture-hardware pair. Actual shapes, kernels, and runtime conditions determine which regime of @tbl-lighthouse-trace applies. Diagnosing whether an execution path is compute-bound, bandwidth-bound, or capacity-bound determines which optimizations yield speedup and which waste engineering effort. Execution time drops most when engineers target the binding term directly rather than distributing effort uniformly.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The bottleneck diagnostic that pairs each binding iron-law term with the optimizations that work and those that are wasted is collected for reference in @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-bottleneck-diagnostic-3fc9.
:::

The remaining four principles of the second question form a tightly coupled diagnostic chain. The Pareto frontier\index{Pareto frontier!multi-objective optimization} (principle \ref{pri-pareto-frontier}) identifies the designs that no alternative beats on every objective at once, and once a design lies on that frontier, improving one objective requires a trade-off against another within the same feasible design set. The arithmetic intensity law\index{Arithmetic intensity!bottleneck diagnosis} (principle \ref{pri-arithmetic-intensity}) diagnoses whether compute or bandwidth sets the ideal ceiling. The energy-movement principle\index{Energy-movement principle!data locality} (principle \ref{pri-energy-movement}) combines per-event costs with event counts. Under the reference energy constants, one DRAM access costs about `{python} EnergyMovementMath.dram_vs_range_mult_str` as much as one arithmetic operation. The lower end is the DRAM-versus-FP32 ratio that anchored hardware acceleration (@sec-hardware-acceleration), and the upper end substitutes the cheaper FP16 operation. Which cost dominates a whole workload still depends on how many of each event occur. Amdahl's Law\index{Amdahl's law!preprocessing bottleneck} (principle \ref{pri-amdahl}) sets the ceiling on any parallelism gain, explaining why data loading and preprocessing can become bottlenecks in highly optimized systems.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The compute-versus-bandwidth-boundary and hardware balance ($\RooflineRidgePoint$) are established in @sec-hardware-acceleration-hardware-balance.
:::

MobileNetV2 touches all four. Depthwise separable convolutions reshape the Pareto frontier [@sandler2018]. INT8 quantization\index{INT8 quantization!bandwidth trade-off} exploits the arithmetic intensity law by raising arithmetic intensity through reduced memory traffic [@jacob2018]. Measured energy savings, where the reduced traffic and supported execution lower total consumption, align with the energy-movement principle, while Amdahl's Law bounds end-to-end speedup when host-side preprocessing remains unaccelerated. Microcontroller workloads such as KWS compress these trade-offs further, operating under sub-megabyte memories that leave little room for avoidable overhead.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Compression moves a model along the accuracy-efficiency frontier, as established in @sec-model-compression-balancing-tradeoffs-6ae3.
:::

### What evidence supports deployment (principles 9–12) {.unnumbered}

The third question concerns failures that bench testing cannot rule out, because a system can work correctly on the bench yet fail silently in production. The verification gap\index{Verification gap!statistical testing} (principle \ref{pri-verification-gap}) specifies the required success probability over a stated deployment population and error tolerance. Testing estimates whether the system meets that requirement, with a separately stated statistical confidence level; it cannot establish correctness for every future input. The statistical drift diagnostic\index{Statistical drift risk!accuracy erosion} (principle \ref{pri-statistical-drift}) detects that the population has changed, and labeled outcomes fit how much that change costs in accuracy. The training-serving skew diagnostic\index{Training-serving skew!accuracy impact} (principle \ref{pri-training-serving-skew}) flags training and serving paths that compute the same features differently. The latency budget\index{Latency budget!tail latency constraint} (principle \ref{pri-latency-budget}) holds serving to the tail quantile the product selects.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Reusing training-time transformation parameters at serving time, the consistency imperative that prevents skew, is established in @sec-data-engineering-ensuring-trainingserving-consistency-c683.
:::

Monitoring infrastructure, drift detection, feature stores, and disaggregated subgroup metrics exist to make these principles measurable and to trigger corrective action. A recommendation system that achieves high offline accuracy still requires parity checks when training-serving skew corrupts feature pipelines (principle \ref{pri-training-serving-skew}) and outcome auditing when user behavior shifts seasonally (principle \ref{pri-statistical-drift}).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The monitoring infrastructure and drift quantification that surface these silent failures are established in @sec-ml-operations-production-monitoring-5e1b.
:::

### The integrated framework {.unnumbered}

The thirteen principles are not a sequence to apply in order. They constrain one another, and a single decision activates several of them in turn.

Quantizing a model from FP16 to INT8 illustrates these mutual constraints in action. This single intervention navigates the Pareto frontier (principle \ref{pri-pareto-frontier}), trading numerical precision for memory traffic, and its consequences spread across the stack. Quantization alters the model's silicon contract (principle \ref{pri-silicon-contract}), shifting its operating point on the arithmetic intensity curve (principle \ref{pri-arithmetic-intensity}) and transforming its energy profile (principle \ref{pri-energy-movement}). In deployment, the latency budget (principle \ref{pri-latency-budget}) dictates whether the resulting speedup meets the service-level objective (SLO), while the verification gap (principle \ref{pri-verification-gap}) demands verifying that the lowered serving graph preserves the empirical accuracy measured during compression testing. The opening fleet failure escaped at exactly this step. Compression testing accepted the quantized model on images from the evaluation pipeline, while the firmware path presented a different population. The training-serving skew diagnostic (principle \ref{pri-training-serving-skew}), comparing model outputs from the two preprocessing paths on the same captured inputs, is the measurement that would have exposed the mismatch before the affected cohort did. In that comparison the evaluation pipeline, which produced the calibration images, plays the role the diagnostic assigns to the training path, and the firmware path plays the serving path. The verification gap names why the failure escaped; the skew diagnostic names how to catch it.

The trace touched seven of the thirteen principles, and which seven depended on the decision. Had the same model moved off the device to a cloud endpoint, data placement (principle \ref{pri-data-gravity}) would have entered, because every input image would then cross the network. Had preprocessing stayed on the host CPU while the NPU ran the faster INT8 kernels, Amdahl's Law (principle \ref{pri-amdahl}) would have bounded how much of that speedup the request path could see. The principles activate in turn as a decision moves from model representation to hardware execution to production validation.

A deployment proposal can be checked against the same principles before anyone writes code.

::: {#chk-conclusion-applying-invariants .callout-checkpoint title="Applying the principles"}

A colleague proposes quantizing your model from FP16 to INT8 to reduce serving costs.

**Trace the principles**

- [ ] **Pareto frontier** (principle \ref{pri-pareto-frontier}): What accuracy are you trading for the bandwidth gain?
- [ ] **Silicon contract** (principle \ref{pri-silicon-contract}): Does the target hardware efficiently accelerate the required INT8 operators?
- [ ] **Verification gap** (principle \ref{pri-verification-gap}): Does the quantized serving artifact preserve the behavior accepted during compression testing?
- [ ] **Training-serving skew** (principle \ref{pri-training-serving-skew}): Do the calibration images pass through the same preprocessing path that every serving device uses?
- [ ] **Latency budget** (principle \ref{pri-latency-budget}): Does the speedup bring you within SLO, or create headroom for batching?

:::

Regrouped by the four parts in which they were introduced, the principles form a cycle rather than a pipeline (@fig-invariants-cycle). The deployment principles (9–13) turn runtime telemetry into evidence that sends work back to the data foundations, so each production lesson becomes the starting condition of the next design pass. The conservation-of-complexity heuristic sits at the center of that cycle because every pass around it asks where the complexity displaced by the previous decision has landed.

That feedback loop is central to production engineering. Principles 9 through 13 expose signals that trigger targeted remediations such as canary rollbacks, fallback heuristics, dataset augmentation, model retraining, or kernel retuning, and the point is to see failures coming before they compound.

::: {#fig-invariants-cycle fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Cycle of ML Systems (13 Principles)**: A four-phase systems engineering lifecycle organized around the conservation-of-complexity heuristic. The phases connect in a feedback cycle, and the thirteen principles sit along the transitions by the part that develops them, spanning bounds, decompositions, fitted models, policy requirements, and design heuristics whose assumptions must be checked. Icons mark the phases: bricks for the data foundations, a neural network for model development, a battery for the efficiency budget of optimization, and a rocket for launch into deployment." fig-alt="Clockwise circular diagram with four phases: Foundations (Data), Development (Model), Optimization (Efficiency), and Deployment (Operations). Arrows connect Foundations to Development, Development to Optimization, Optimization to Deployment, and Deployment back to Foundations. The transitions are labeled 1–2 Data as Code and data gravity; 3–4 iron law and Silicon Contract; 5–8 Pareto Frontier, Arithmetic Intensity, Energy-Movement, and Amdahl’s Law; and 9–13 verification gap, Statistical Drift, Skew Diagnostic, Latency Budget, and Bias Feedback. A dashed center circle is labeled Conservation of Complexity."}
